title: Passage planning and heavy weather
summary: Building a weather picture, choosing a window, ports of refuge, and heavy-weather preparation and tactics.

segments.heading: Building the picture
paragraphs: Start several days out: follow the synoptic and forecast charts to understand the pattern and how it is evolving. Closer to departure, add the official marine forecast, inshore forecasts, gale warnings and GRIB data from more than one model. Note where forecasts disagree; disagreement is a measure of uncertainty.

Then apply it to your boat and crew. What is the strongest likely wind including gusts, from which direction relative to your course and the tidal streams, for how long, and with what sea state at headlands and in the approach to your destination?
keyPoints: Follow the pattern for days, not just the latest forecast.
Model disagreement means uncertainty: add margin.
Translate wind and sea into conditions on your route.

segments.heading: Limits, timing and refuges
paragraphs: Set personal limits for wind, sea and visibility before you read the forecast, and agree them with the crew. Time departure so that the passage ends in daylight and the worst of any front or wind shift is met in open water, not at a lee-shore harbour entrance.

List ports of refuge along the route, noting which are safe to enter in the forecast wind direction, at what states of tide, and in darkness. Remember that a forecast veer can turn a refuge into a dangerous entrance.

segments.heading: Set your limits before you look
paragraphs: Decide your limits before reading the forecast, so the forecast cannot talk you into going. For this boat and crew: the strongest wind including gusts, the highest sea state, wind direction relative to the course, minimum visibility, and whether you will arrive in daylight. Lower the limits for a tired, inexperienced or small crew.

Then check the forecast against those limits for the whole passage plus a margin, not just the departure time. Identify fallback ports you can reach in the forecast wind, and the point beyond which turning back is no longer the safer option.
keyPoints: Fix limits first: wind and gusts, sea, direction, visibility, daylight.
Check the whole passage plus a margin.
Name fallback ports and the point of no return.

segments.heading: Triggers, and motor versus sail
paragraphs: Agree triggers for changing the plan before you leave: a new warning, the barometer falling faster than forecast, the wind or sea above your limits, slower progress than planned, or a tiring crew. When a trigger is met, act on it; do not wait for the next forecast.

Boat type changes the decision. A motor cruiser can use speed to fit a short window, but must slow right down in head seas, depends on fuel and on the engine, and can broach in steep following seas. A sailing yacht is slower, so stays exposed for longer, but can keep moving without the engine. Base the plan on realistic speed in the expected sea, not on flat-water speed.
keyPoints: Agree triggers in advance and act when one is met.
Plan on realistic speed in the expected sea.
Motor: speed, fuel, head and following seas. Sail: longer exposure.

segments.heading: Before it arrives
paragraphs: Reef early. Stow and secure everything below and on deck, close hatches and seacocks not in use, rig jackstays and ensure everyone wears lifejackets and harnesses on deck. Prepare hot food and drinks and simple snacks, set a watch rota that protects the crew from fatigue, and brief everyone on the plan and on seasickness management.
Fix your position and plan sea room: the greatest danger in heavy weather is usually the land, not the sea.
keyPoints: Reef early and secure the boat.
Feed and rest the crew; keep sea room.

segments.heading: Tactics
paragraphs: A sailing yacht's options include continuing under deeply reefed sail; heaving-to, which on many boats (backed headsail, eased main, helm to windward) slows her to a slow drift to leeward and lets the crew rest, but which depends on the boat and rig, needs sea room and may not suit breaking seas; running off under minimal sail, with warps or a drogue to control speed; and, in survival conditions, a sea anchor. Drogues and sea anchors need gear matched to the boat and practice before you need them. A motor boat's options are different, usually holding a chosen angle to the sea at reduced speed. Practise any tactic in moderate conditions first.

There is no universal tactic. The right choice depends on sail or power, hull form and stability, the size, shape and period of the seas, sea room, visibility, the crew and the builder's guidance. Better still, avoid it: divert or seek shelter early, reduce speed and reassess often, and decide while the crew still has energy.

questions.prompt: Three models disagree by 12 hours on when a front will arrive. What does this tell you?
options: Use the most optimistic model
Forecast uncertainty is high; build in a margin or wait
Average them and leave on the average
Ignore models and use the barometer only
optionExplanations: Picking the best case is wishful thinking.
Correct.
An average hides the spread.
The barometer complements, not replaces, forecasts.
questions.explanation: Disagreement between models quantifies uncertainty. Plan for the earlier arrival or delay.

questions.prompt: When should you set your personal wind limits for a passage?
options: After reading the forecast
Before reading the forecast
Once at sea
Only if a gale is forecast
optionExplanations: That invites talking yourself into it.
Correct.
Too late.
Limits apply to all conditions.
questions.explanation: Fixed limits set in advance protect against optimistic reading of a marginal forecast.

questions.prompt: A gale is forecast in 8 hours and you are committed to the passage. Which preparations should you make now? Select all that apply.
options: Reef before the wind rises
Prepare hot food and flasks
Open hatches for ventilation
Rig jackstays and wear harnesses
Plan to stay well offshore away from a lee shore
optionExplanations: Correct.
Correct.
Hatches must be closed and secured.
Correct.
Correct: sea room is safety.
questions.explanation: Prepare the boat, the crew and the plan before conditions deteriorate.

questions.prompt: What is heaving-to on a typical sailing yacht?
options: Running downwind under bare poles
Backed headsail, eased mainsail and helm to windward, so the boat lies quietly with a slow drift to leeward
Motoring into the wind at full power
Anchoring in deep water
optionExplanations: That is running off.
Correct.
Not heaving-to.
Not heaving-to.
questions.explanation: On many yachts heaving-to slows the boat to a slow drift and lets the crew rest. It needs sea room, depends on the boat and rig, may not suit breaking seas, and should be practised first.

questions.context: You plan a 60-mile passage along a south-facing coast. Forecast: 'West 4 to 5, increasing 6 to 7 later, veering north-west.' Your planned destination harbour has a bar entrance facing west, dangerous in strong westerlies and on the ebb. An alternative harbour, 40 miles along, faces south-east with an all-tide entrance.
questions.explanation: Avoid the exposed west-facing bar in a rising westerly; the south-east-facing harbour is sheltered from the forecast west to north-west wind.

steps.prompt: Why is the planned destination a poor choice?
options: The bar faces the rising westerly and may break on the ebb
It is too far
It has no fuel
Harbours are always dangerous at night
optionExplanations: Correct.
Distance is not the main issue.
Irrelevant to safety here.
Too general.
steps.explanation: A west-facing bar with a strong westerly and an ebb running out can break dangerously.

steps.prompt: Will the south-east-facing harbour stay sheltered after the veer to north-west?
options: Yes: its entrance faces away from both westerly and north-westerly winds
No: the veer makes it a lee shore
Only at high water
Only in daylight
optionExplanations: Correct.
A north-westerly blows offshore at a south-east-facing entrance.
It is an all-tide entrance.
Not the deciding factor.
steps.explanation: An entrance facing south-east is in the lee of both west and north-west winds.

steps.prompt: What is the sound decision?
options: Plan for the alternative harbour as the destination from the start
Head for the bar and decide on arrival
Delay until the gale is blowing to check its strength
Anchor off the bar
optionExplanations: Correct: shorter, sheltered, all-tide.
Deciding at a breaking bar is too late.
Waiting into the gale reduces options.
An open anchorage off a lee bar is dangerous.
steps.explanation: Choose the destination that stays safe in the forecast's worst stage.

questions.prompt: In heavy weather offshore, what is usually the greatest danger?
options: The waves themselves
The land: a lee shore and loss of sea room
Running out of food
Cold
optionExplanations: Waves are a risk, but well-found boats cope with sea room.
Correct.
Manageable with preparation.
Manageable with clothing.
questions.explanation: Sea room is safety. Most heavy-weather losses involve the land.

questions.prompt: Running off before large breaking seas, the boat is surfing dangerously fast. What helps?
options: Hoisting more sail
Streaming warps or a drogue to slow her
Steering exactly square to every crest at full speed
Turning beam-on to the seas
optionExplanations: More sail increases speed.
Correct.
Excess speed risks pitchpoling or broaching.
Beam-on risks a knockdown.
questions.explanation: Controlling speed with drag devices reduces the risk of broaching or pitchpoling.

questions.prompt: Conditions are worse than forecast and the crew is tiring. What is the seamanlike response?
options: Press on to the plan
Reassess: divert, heave-to or turn back as needed
Increase sail to arrive sooner
Wait for the next forecast before doing anything
optionExplanations: The plan was based on a forecast that is now wrong.
Correct.
More sail adds risk.
Act on what you see now.
questions.explanation: Changing plan in response to conditions is good seamanship.

questions.context: In May you plan to sail west from Weymouth to Dartmouth: about 8 miles to Portland Bill, then about 47 miles across Lyme Bay. Boat: 10 m yacht, crew of three. Your limits: Force 6, moderate sea, arrive before dark (sunset about 21:00). HW Dover is 11:00. The almanac advises rounding the Bill westbound, close in by the inshore passage, between HW Dover −1 and +2 (10:00 to 13:00); the stream off the Bill then sets west until about 16:00. You leave Weymouth at 09:00. Forecast for the sea area, issued 05:00: 'West or south-west 4 or 5, occasionally 6 later. Moderate. Fair. Good.'
questions.explanation: The competence being tested is reassessment: when a new warning and the arithmetic show your limits will be broken, choose the safest reachable refuge rather than pressing on.

steps.prompt: How do you plan the rounding of Portland Bill?
options: Through the race around 14:00, with the strongest westgoing stream
By the inshore passage between 10:00 and 13:00 as the almanac advises, or well outside the race
At 16:00, whatever the wind
Ignore the race: Force 4 to 5 is moderate
optionExplanations: A westerly wind blows towards the east, against the strong westgoing stream: steep breaking seas in the race.
Correct: the recommended window, close in, or a wide berth outside the race.
The stream turns about then; timing must suit both stream and wind.
Races can be dangerous in moderate winds.
steps.explanation: Use the almanac's westbound window for the inshore passage, or keep well outside the race.

steps.prompt: At 11:00, abeam the Bill, a gale warning is broadcast: 'Westerly gale 8 expected later'. When is the gale expected?
options: Within 6 hours
6 to 12 hours
More than 12 hours after issue
It is already blowing
optionExplanations: That is 'imminent'.
That is 'soon'.
Correct: 'later' means more than 12 hours after issue.
Not yet.
steps.explanation: 'Later' is more than 12 hours from the time of issue.

steps.prompt: Dartmouth is about 47 miles on. Beating into the westerly your speed made good is 4 knots. How many hours to arrive?
steps.explanation: 47 ÷ 4 is about 11¾ hours: arriving around 22:45, well after dark, as the wind rises.

steps.prompt: At 11:00 you are just past the Bill. Which decision is best supported by the evidence?
options: Press on: the gale is not due until after 23:00
Reassess and head for the nearest suitable refuge, most likely Weymouth: about 9 miles back, downwind and sheltered from the west
Heave to off the Bill and wait for a later forecast
Motor into it at full power to arrive before dark
optionExplanations: The gale may hold off, but you would beat for nearly 12 hours into a rising wind and arrive well after dark, breaking your daylight limit.
Correct: your daylight limit will be broken and the wind is forecast to rise; check the stream and the race before turning.
Close to the race and with a rising westerly; it does not solve the daylight problem.
Head seas will slow you and tire the crew; arrival before dark is not realistic.
steps.explanation: The gale timing alone does not decide it: a beat of nearly 12 hours into a rising wind, arriving after dark, breaks your limits. The nearest refuge sheltered from the west is the better choice.

questions.context: July, in the Cyclades. You plan to sail from Kythnos east to Syros, about 25 miles, a beam reach of about five hours. Your crew of four includes two beginners, and your limit is Force 6. The national forecast for the area: 'Today: North 4 to 5 Beaufort, locally 6 in the afternoon. Tomorrow and the following day: North 6 to 7, locally 8.'
questions.explanation: Go/no-go comes first: today is within your limits and the next days are not. Leave early, expect acceleration and lee gusts, check any anchorage for more than wind direction, and stay put when the forecast exceeds your limits.

steps.prompt: Today's forecast is within your limits; the next two days are not. What is the best plan?
options: Go today, leaving at first light to arrive before the afternoon wind
Go today, leaving after lunch
Wait in Kythnos and sail tomorrow
Go today, leaving at dusk when the wind usually drops
optionExplanations: Correct: within limits, and arriving before the usual afternoon peak.
You would be crossing during the windiest part of the day.
Tomorrow's forecast is above your limits; waiting means a longer delay.
Arriving at an unfamiliar island in the dark adds risk, and the wind may not drop.
steps.explanation: Decide go/no-go first; then, if you go, time the passage to finish before the afternoon peak.

steps.prompt: Where on the route should you expect the strongest gusts?
options: Nowhere in particular: the Meltemi is uniform
In the channel between the islands, off the capes, and in gusts falling off high ground in the lee
Only in Syros harbour
Only in open water far from the islands
optionExplanations: Islands make it very uneven.
Correct: channel and cape acceleration, plus violent downslope gusts in the lee.
Harbours are usually sheltered, though gusts can reach them.
The islands are where the wind is squeezed and accelerated.
steps.explanation: Expect a force or more extra in channels and off capes, and a calm close under high ground can turn into violent gusts.

steps.prompt: You reach Syros. Which is the soundest way to choose shelter for the night?
options: Any bay open to the north, for the breeze
A harbour or bay sheltered from the north, after checking the pilot for downslope gusts, swell, holding and a way out
Any bay, since the wind drops at night
An open roadstead on the east coast
optionExplanations: Open to the Meltemi and its sea.
Correct: shelter from the north is the start; then check the local hazards.
It may not drop, and can blow all night.
Exposed to swell working round the island.
steps.explanation: A lee can be untenable in violent downslope gusts; a harbour may be better than an anchorage.

steps.prompt: Next morning in Syros the forecast is confirmed: 'North 6 to 7, locally 8'. With two beginners aboard, what do you do?
options: Sail as planned
Stay in harbour and wait for the Meltemi to ease
Leave at noon to cross faster
Motor directly into it
optionExplanations: Above sensible limits for this crew.
Correct: Meltemi spells end; waiting costs only time.
The strongest part of the day.
Head seas and wind beyond limits.
steps.explanation: Stay put when the forecast exceeds your crew's limits.

questions.prompt: A motor cruiser (cruising at 18 knots) and a sailing yacht (6 knots) plan the same 36-mile passage in a 4-hour window before a front. Which statement is right?
options: Both have plenty of time
The motor cruiser fits the window only if it can keep its speed in the expected sea
The yacht is safer because it is slower
Neither should consider speed
optionExplanations: The yacht needs about 6 hours: it does not fit.
Correct: head seas can halve a planing boat's speed.
Slower means longer exposure.
Realistic speed is central to the decision.
questions.explanation: Plan on realistic speed in the expected sea; the yacht does not fit this window at all.

questions.context: Boat: 9 m planing motor cruiser, about 20 knots in calm water, crew of two. You plan to go from the Hamble to Poole, about 30 miles, leaving the Solent through Hurst Narrows and the Needles Channel. HW Portsmouth is 10:00. In Hurst Narrows the stream sets south-west from about 09:00 (HW Portsmouth −1) to about 15:15 (HW Portsmouth +5¼), up to 4 knots at springs. Forecast: 'South-west 5 to 6, occasionally 7 later. Moderate or rough.'
questions.explanation: A motor boat's speed only helps if the sea allows it. Time the tidal gate for the sea state, plan on realistic speed, and keep the Solent harbours as refuges.

steps.prompt: When is the sea in the Needles Channel likely to be worst?
options: While the south-west-going ebb runs against the south-westerly wind
While the north-east-going flood runs with the wind
At slack water
It makes no difference
optionExplanations: Correct: wind against a strong stream over shallow ground.
Wind and stream together give a longer, easier sea.
Usually the easiest time.
Stream direction changes the sea a great deal.
steps.explanation: A south-westerly blows towards the north-east, against the south-west-going ebb: expect steep, breaking seas.

steps.prompt: Beyond Hurst, the head sea forces you off the plane to 8 knots. How long will the remaining 15 miles to Poole take, in hours?
steps.explanation: 15 ÷ 8 is just under 2 hours, against 45 minutes at planing speed. Check fuel and arrival time on realistic speed, not calm-water speed.

steps.prompt: At 10:30, approaching Hurst, you see breaking seas in the Needles Channel. What do you do?
options: Drive through at full speed to get it over quickly
Turn back to Yarmouth or Lymington and wait for the stream to turn, about 15:15, then reassess with the latest forecast
Slow right down and go through anyway
Anchor off Hurst Castle and watch
optionExplanations: Speed into steep breaking seas risks damage and injury.
Correct: sheltered refuges close by; the sea will ease when the stream turns, if the wind allows.
Breaking seas over shallow ground are the hazard, whatever the speed.
Exposed, in a strong stream, close to the hazard.
steps.explanation: Use a nearby refuge and the tidal timing rather than forcing a tidal gate in breaking seas.

questions.context: Late August. You plan to take a 12 m yacht with an experienced crew of four from Chania to Piraeus, about 140 miles north, with Milos roughly halfway. The national marine forecast: 'Cretan Sea and southern Aegean: North 6 to 7 Beaufort, locally 8, easing to North 3 to 4 from the day after tomorrow for about two days.' Your limits: Force 6 on the nose, and no night arrivals in unfamiliar harbours.
questions.explanation: Heading north from Crete in summer usually means heading into the Meltemi. Wait for a lull, split the passage, expect leftover sea, and re-check the forecast at each stop.

steps.prompt: What do you do now?
options: Leave today and beat north
Leave today and motor straight into it
Wait in Chania for the forecast lull
Leave tonight, when the wind may ease
optionExplanations: 140 miles to windward in Force 6 to 7, locally 8: beyond your limits.
Head seas and wind beyond limits, for many hours.
Correct: the lull is forecast within two days.
It may ease, but the forecast is for the whole period and you would be at sea at night.
steps.explanation: Go/no-go first: the forecast exceeds your limits, and a lull is coming.

steps.prompt: The lull arrives. Which plan fits a two-day window best?
options: Non-stop, 140 miles
Two legs via Milos, about 70 miles each, with a stop to rest and get a fresh forecast
Daylight hops of 20 miles
Via Kythira
optionExplanations: About 24 hours or more at sea, with no chance to re-check the forecast.
Correct: each leg fits in daylight and gives a decision point.
Too slow to finish inside the window.
Well off the direct route.
steps.explanation: Splitting the passage gives rest and a fresh go/no-go decision halfway.

steps.prompt: Leaving Chania on the first morning of the lull, what sea do you expect?
options: Flat calm
A leftover northerly sea and swell, on the nose, easing through the day
A southerly swell
None at all
optionExplanations: Several days of strong northerlies leave a sea behind.
Correct: waves built over a long fetch take time to die down.
The wind has been from the north.
Not after days of strong wind.
steps.explanation: The sea lags the wind: expect a head sea for some hours after the wind eases.

steps.prompt: At Milos the new forecast brings the next Meltemi forward to the evening of your planned second leg. What do you do?
options: Press on regardless
Leave at first light only if you can reach Piraeus with a clear margin before the wind returns; otherwise wait in Milos
Leave in the afternoon
Ignore it: forecasts are often wrong
optionExplanations: The plan was built on the old forecast.
Correct: reassess against your limits and the new timing.
You would meet the returning wind at sea, at night.
Plan to the official forecast, and watch for it changing.
steps.explanation: Each stop is a new go/no-go decision against the latest forecast.

questions.context: Early April. You plan to sail a 10 m yacht from Chania north-west to Kythira, about 60 miles, across the open water between western Crete and the Peloponnese. A depression over the Ionian Sea is moving east. Forecast: 'South-east 5 to 6, increasing 7 for a time, veering west 6 to 7 after a cold front passes tomorrow afternoon. Rough, locally very rough.' Crew of three; limits Force 6.
questions.explanation: Both phases of this system exceed the limits: a strong south-easterly and large following sea before the front, then a westerly and a cross sea after it. Wait for it to clear.

steps.prompt: Where are you relative to the system today?
options: Behind the cold front
Ahead of the cold front, in the south-easterly flow
Under an anticyclone
In a col
optionExplanations: The veer to the west has not happened yet.
Correct: south-easterly ahead of the front, veering west as it passes.
Pressure is falling with a depression approaching.
There is a clear gradient.
steps.explanation: South-easterly winds ahead of an approaching front, with a veer to the west to come.

steps.prompt: What sea would you meet on the passage today?
options: A short northerly sea
A large following sea from the south-east, built over a long fetch, with a risk of broaching
Calm water in the lee of Crete
Only a westerly sea
optionExplanations: The wind is from the south-east.
Correct: steep following seas make steering hard and broaching likely.
Your route leaves the lee of Crete quickly.
That comes after the front.
steps.explanation: A long open fetch to the south-east builds a large sea that you would have astern.

steps.prompt: What is the seamanlike decision?
options: Go now to arrive before the front
Wait in Chania until the front has passed and the sea has eased
Go just after the front, into the westerly
Go tonight
optionExplanations: Force 7 and a very rough following sea are beyond your limits.
Correct: both phases exceed your limits; this system will pass.
Westerly 6 to 7 over a big leftover south-easterly swell gives a confused cross sea.
Night adds risk without solving the weather.
steps.explanation: No departure time makes this passage fit the limits; wait for the system to clear.

steps.prompt: When you do go, how should you choose the harbour on Kythira?
options: The nearest one, whatever its exposure
Check its exposure to the wind and swell expected on arrival and overnight, and whether it can be entered safely in those conditions
Any harbour, since the wind will have eased
Only by its facilities
optionExplanations: The nearest may be open to the wind or swell.
Correct: exposure and entry conditions decide it, using the pilot.
Swell can persist long after the wind eases.
Facilities do not make a harbour safe.
steps.explanation: Choose a refuge for the wind and swell you expect, not for distance alone.
